sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Module overview and imports
sections.what: Nothing runs here. It explains the formulas and the meaning of the day counts, and loads the helper tools.
sections.why: Gives the reader the formulas before the code.

sections.name: calculate_ar
sections.title: Money owed by customers each year
sections.what: Works out the yearly receivable balance from revenue and the days it usually takes to collect payment.
sections.why: Likely reason: unpaid sales are income the company has earned but not yet received.
sections.watch_out: The days value must be a count of days; a rate typed in its place gives wrong balances.

sections.name: calculate_inventory
sections.title: Stock held each year
sections.what: Works out the value of stock held, based on cost of goods and the days of stock held.
sections.why: Likely reason: stock is cash already spent but not yet sold, so it ties up money.
sections.watch_out: It is based on cost of goods rather than sales, so a change in selling prices alone does not change stock.

sections.name: calculate_ap
sections.title: Money owed to suppliers each year
sections.what: Works out what the company owes suppliers, based on cost of goods and the days taken to pay.
sections.why: Likely reason: unpaid supplier bills give the business a free source of funding.
sections.watch_out: A longer payment period lowers cash needs, so a wrong days figure can make cash look better than it is.

sections.name: calculate_working_capital_full
sections.title: Net working capital and yearly change
sections.what: Combines receivables and stock, subtracts payables, then works out the year-to-year change in that net figure.
sections.why: The yearly change is what affects cash, so it is calculated here.
sections.watch_out: The change list has one fewer entry than the others, so the first year has no change figure.

summary: Works out how much money is tied up in customer bills, stock, and supplier bills each year, and how that amount changes from one year to the next.
purpose: Produces receivables, inventory, payables, net working capital, and the yearly change.
why: Money tied up in unpaid bills and stock affects cash, so the cash flow needs the yearly change.
how: 1. Receivables equal revenue times days to collect, divided by 365. 2. Inventory equals cost of goods times days of stock, divided by 365. 3. Payables equal cost of goods times days to pay suppliers, divided by 365. 4. Net working capital equals receivables plus inventory minus payables. 5. The change is the difference from one year to the next.
inputs: Revenue list; cost of goods list; days sales outstanding; days inventory held; days payable outstanding.
outputs: Receivables, inventory, payables, and net working capital lists, plus a change list that is one item shorter.
risks: The 365-day year is fixed in the code. The change list is one item shorter than the others, so it does not line up by year without an adjustment.
debug: Check the days inputs first. If cash flow looks wrong, compare the change list with the difference in net working capital between years.
